declarations.name: supportsInvokers
declarations.description:
Whether the browser implements invoker commands.

Feature-detected on the prototype rather than on an instance, so it can be
answered before anything has rendered, and guarded for a server, which has no
`HTMLButtonElement` at all.

The `command` event, for a browser that does not send one.

Invoker commands are recent: Chrome 135, Firefox 137, Safari 18.4. Before
this, a button in an older browser set `commandForElement` on nothing, the
wiring silently did not happen, and the control did nothing at all when
clicked. No error, no warning, and every `command` in the library dead at
once, which is the worst way for a feature to be missing: the markup is
right, the component is right, and the button is simply inert.

So the button sends this instead where the platform will not. It carries the
two members `CommandController` reads and dispatches at the target, which is
where the platform dispatches too, so nothing downstream can tell the
difference.

**The built-in commands are not reproduced.** `show-modal`, `close` and
`toggle-popover` are defined against native elements and applied by the
browser itself, and writing our own would mean reimplementing part of the
platform against elements we do not own. Nothing in this library uses them:
a custom element only ever answers a `--` command, which is the platform's
marker for "the target decides", and the target is ours.
declarations.name: HelixFallbackCommandEvent

members.name: command
members.description: The command asked for, verbatim.

members.name: source
members.description: The element that asked.

declarations.description:
Lets a control elsewhere on the page operate this one, declaratively.

```html
<helix-button commandfor="confirm" command="--show">Delete…</helix-button>
<helix-dialog id="confirm">…</helix-dialog>
```

**The platform's own invoker, not a convention of ours.** `commandfor` and
`command` are attributes the browser understands: it resolves the id, wires
the two together, and dispatches a `command` event at the target when the
trigger is activated. That is a real event with a real source, so it works
for a click, for Enter, for Space, and for anything else the platform decides
counts as activation later.

The alternative was a `data-` recipe of our own with a delegated listener on
the document, and it is worse in every direction: a global listener a
consumer cannot see, an id lookup we would write ourselves, activation
semantics we would have to guess at, and a convention that is ours to
document and theirs to learn.

**Only custom commands reach a custom element.** The built-in ones —
`show-modal`, `close`, `toggle-popover` — are defined against native elements
and the browser applies them itself; pointed at a custom element they do
nothing. So the names here start with `--`, which is the platform's marker
for "the target decides what this means", and the target deciding is exactly
what this is.

Unrecognised commands are left alone rather than swallowed, so a host that
answers `--show` does not quietly absorb a `--print` meant for something
else.
declarations.name: CommandController

declarations.description:
Pushes a group's `disabled` onto its members, on every update, unasked.

**The cascade itself is `inheritDisabled`, and this is what makes it
automatic.** Four groups called that function by hand from inside whichever
method they happened to use for writing to their items: `place` in two of
them, `sync` in a third, `place` again in the fourth. That works, and it is
the wrong shape for three reasons.

It runs when that method runs. A group whose items changed without going
through it left them holding the last answer, and which paths reach it is a
different set in each of the four.

It has to be remembered. A fifth group gets no cascade at all, and nothing
says so: the property exists, the attribute reflects, and the members simply
ignore it. That is the failure this exists to make impossible, because it is
invisible in review and only shows up when someone disables a set.

And it adds no API. A group already has `disabled`, from `HelixFormElement`
or from the consumer; nothing here introduces a property or a method for
anyone to call. By this repo's own rule that makes it a controller and not a
mixin: it reacts to a lifecycle and nothing else.

So a group states its members once, at construction, and never thinks about
it again:

    new DisabledCascadeController(this, { items: () => this.items })

**Runs after every render, and on every `slotchange`.** The second half is
not an extra: a member arriving in the light DOM changes no property, so Lit
schedules nothing, and a render-only cascade leaves a member slotted into an
already-disabled group enabled. Measured before it was added, on a radio
group holding two disabled members with a third inserted: `110`, and the
third was live in a set nobody could use.

The listener is on the render root rather than on the host, because
`slotchange` bubbles but is not composed: it reaches the shadow root that
owns the slot and stops there. On the host it would never fire at all.

After render rather than before, because the items are read from the DOM and
a newly slotted member is not there until the render that assigns it.

Idempotent, so running on every update costs a comparison per member and
nothing else: `inheritDisabled` writes only where the answer changed and
remembers what each member said for itself, which is what lets a group be
re-enabled without freeing a member that was disabled on its own.
declarations.name: DisabledCascadeController

declarations.description:
Closes an overlay on Escape or on a pointer press outside it.

Both, because they are different intentions with the same meaning: Escape is
the keyboard's way out and clicking away is the pointer's, and an overlay
that honours only one is one half its readers cannot dismiss.

The outside press is watched on `pointerdown` rather than `click`, so a press
that starts outside and drags across the overlay still counts as leaving
rather than as interacting.

A press inside a frame is the third case, and it needs its own signal. The
frame swallows the event, so the document that owns the overlay never sees a
`pointerdown` at all, and where the frame is cross-origin there is nothing to
listen to inside it either. What is observable is that the window lost focus
and a frame on this page gained it, which is exactly a press the document
cannot see. Leaving the browser altogether blurs the window too, so what took
focus is the part that distinguishes them.
declarations.name: DismissController

members.name: handleWindowBlur
members.description:
Focus left the document. If a frame took it, that was a press.

Deferred by a task, because the order of `blur` against the focus moving is
not something every browser agrees on and reading `activeElement` too early
gives the element that is losing focus rather than the one taking it. The
guard is for the case where the overlay closed for another reason in
between, which would otherwise dismiss whatever opened next.

declarations.description:
One page of a nested set showing at a time, with a way back.

A drill-down replaces the panel rather than opening a second one beside it.
That is the right shape wherever there is no room for two: on a phone there
is no second column, and on a touch screen there is no hover to open one
with. What a reader gets instead is one panel, a title saying where they are,
and a way back.

**Extracted from `Menu`, which had all of this and did not say so.** The menu
held a `page`, derived the rows on it, read a title off the row that opened
it, and reset on close; the sandbox's settings dropdown has been a drill-down
for as long as it has existed. None of that is about menus. Taking it out is
what lets a settings panel, a filter stack or a navigation tree have the same
behavior without one of them being a menu that is pretending.

**The tree is the state.** A row's page is its own children, assigned to a
slot, so the controller holds one reference, the row currently drilled into,
and derives everything else from the DOM. The alternative, an id per page and
a map beside it, is a second copy of the structure that a consumer can put
out of step with the first.

**A stack, not a pointer.** `back()` returns to the page above rather than to
the root, because a reader three levels down pressed one control and expects
one level. The stack is rebuilt from the DOM by walking up from the current
row, so it cannot disagree with the tree: a page removed while it was showing
takes its ancestors with it, and `atRoot` becomes true rather than the
controller holding a reference to something detached.

Nothing here decides what a row *is*, what it renders, or what happens when
one is chosen. It answers where the reader is and what is on this page.
declarations.name: DrilldownController

declarations.description:
Places one element against another, and keeps it there.

Positioning is `@floating-ui/dom` rather than arithmetic written here. Two
things in particular are why. A `position: fixed` element inside an ancestor
carrying `transform`, `filter`, `will-change`, or `contain` is positioned
against that ancestor and not the viewport, so viewport coordinates land it
somewhere else entirely. And an overlay has to clear its nearest *clipping*
ancestor, not just the window, or it is placed correctly inside a scrolling
panel and clipped out of sight by it. Both are ordinary here, and both are a
long tail of browser behavior rather than a formula.

`autoUpdate` keeps the position through scrolling on any ancestor, resizes of
either element, and layout shifts.

The side the element actually landed on is written back as `data-placement`,
so a styled tier can animate from it rather than from the side that was
asked for.
declarations.name: FloatingController

Keeps Tab inside a container while it is open, and gives focus back after.

A dialog that does not trap focus is one a keyboard user tabs straight out
of, into a page they cannot see and cannot get back from. Restoring focus on
release matters just as much: without it, closing a drawer drops the reader
at the top of the document.

Finding the focusable elements is `focusableElements`, which is a utility
rather than part of this, because that half is what roving tabindex and
arrow-key navigation need and neither of them traps anything.
declarations.name: FocusTrapController

members.name: activate

declarations.description:
Measures the marked child and writes the geometry onto a travelling mark.

**Four components had written this and the copies had diverged.** `NavBar`,
`Tabs`, `Toggle.Group` and `PageNav` each measured an active child and wrote
a position onto an indicator, and two of them had bugs the others did not.
`PageNav`'s own comment counted the repetition rather than resolving it, and
the audit found the same shape independently in all four.

What the copies disagreed about, and what this settles:

**The inline axis is signed.** In a right-to-left document the distance is
measured from the surface's right edge and applied as a negative translation,
because the mark travels from the inline start and the inline start is on the
right. `NavBar` measured from the physical left and applied it from the
inline-start edge with an unsigned offset, so its marker went the wrong way
in RTL. That is the bug this extraction exists to stop repeating.

**The border has to come off both axes.** `getBoundingClientRect` gives the
border box and the containing block is the padding box, so a surface with a
border of its own puts the mark one border-width out. `Tabs` and
`Toggle.Group` each did this arithmetic separately, `PageNav` did the block
half with `clientTop`, and `NavBar` did neither. `clientLeft` and `clientTop`
are the border widths, already resolved, which is why they are used here
rather than parsing `borderLeftWidth`.

**Nothing is written until there is something to measure.** A zero-width box
is a component whose children have not upgraded yet, and writing zeroes would
park the mark at the origin and leave it there. The `data-placed` attribute is
what a stylesheet waits for, so a mark fades in where it belongs rather than
sliding from the corner on first paint.

The four custom properties are the contract: `--_indicator-x`, `-y`, `-w` and
`-h`. What a component does with them is its own business, which is how one
controller serves a bar under a tab, a pill filling it, and a rule down the
side of a contents page.
declarations.name: IndicatorController

members.name: hostUpdated
members.description: Called after every update, which is when the marked child may have moved.

members.name: place
members.description:
Measures and writes, or gives up without writing anything.

Public because `slotchange` is not an update: children arriving is exactly
when the first measurement becomes possible, and a component that only
placed on its own updates left the mark unplaced for the life of the page.

declarations.description:
Moves through a set of items with the arrow keys, and chooses as it goes.

**Moving and choosing are one act here, not two.** That is the radio group
pattern and it is the difference from a listbox: moving focus without
choosing leaves a keyboard reader sitting on an item they have not selected,
with nothing on screen saying which of the two is true. A pointer user
chooses by arriving, so a keyboard user does too.

**Both axes, always.** A vertical set still answers left and right, and a
horizontal one still answers up and down. Binding only the axis the items
happen to be laid out on means a reader who guesses wrong gets nothing, and
`orientation` is presentation: the same set of choices reads the same way
whichever direction it runs.

Disabled items are skipped rather than stopped at, so a set with a gap in it
still moves in one press.

Written because `Radio.Group` and `Toggle.Group` had this twice, identically,
down to the order of the branches. The second copy is what makes it a
controller: one is a component's own business, two is a pattern, and the two
had not diverged only because nothing had touched them yet.
declarations.name: KeyboardNavigationController

declarations.description:
A surface that floats against something, in the top layer, until dismissed.

Three things always travel together and were written out longhand three
times: the popover API, a `FloatingController` and a `DismissController`.
Individually each is small, which is exactly why the copies drifted rather
than being noticed. **`Select` never called `showPopover` at all**, so its
list was an ordinary positioned panel and any ancestor with `overflow:
hidden` clipped it, while a menu two folders away in the same position did
not. That is not a difference anyone chose.

**The top layer is the whole point.** A floating panel has to escape every
clipping ancestor between it and the page, and `position: fixed` does not do
that: it is clipped by `overflow` on any ancestor and re-anchored entirely by
an ancestor carrying `transform`, `filter` or `contain`. The popover API
lifts the element out of the tree's paint order for real, and it is the only
thing that does.

`manual` rather than `auto`, because the host owns dismissal. `auto`
popovers light-dismiss themselves and close each other, which is close to
what is wanted and not the same: a select that closed itself before its own
change event landed, or a submenu that closed its parent, are both things the
platform would do here and neither is right.

**The order matters on the way up.** `showPopover` first, then position:
measuring an element that is still `display: none` gives zeroes, so a surface
positioned before it is shown lands at the origin and slides into place on
the next frame. On the way down it is the reverse, and stopping the observer
before hiding avoids a final measurement of an element on its way out.

What this does not own is *when*. Opening is the host's, because a menu opens
on click, a tooltip on hover and a select on either, and none of that is
about surfaces.
declarations.name: PopoverController

Shows the surface, positions it, and starts listening for a way out.

Safe to call when already open, so a host may call it from whatever
combination of a property, an event and a command it likes without keeping

members.description:
Leaves the top layer when the host does.

An element removed while its popover is showing is removed from the top
layer by the platform, but the controllers watching it are this host's to
stop, and `autoUpdate` in particular holds listeners on every scrolling
ancestor of something no longer in the document.

declarations.description:
Fired when an element is about to open.

Cancelable: `preventDefault()` refuses the change, and the element stays
closed. Paired with `helix-close` rather than being one event carrying a
boolean, so a listener that only cares about one direction says so by which
event it listens for.

Neither bubbles nor composed. A dialog inside a drawer inside a popover is
three overlays, and an inner one opening must not read as the outer one
opening.
declarations.name: HelixOpenEvent

declarations.description: Fired when an element is about to close. See `HelixOpenEvent`.
declarations.name: HelixCloseEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when an element asks to be taken away.

A request rather than a notification: the element does not remove itself,
because the consumer owns the markup it is in and removing the node under
them would put their state and the document out of step. Cancelable, so
`preventDefault()` is a refusal.

One verb for both shapes. A tag leaving a list and an announcement closing
itself are the same act from the element's side.
declarations.name: HelixDismissEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when a value changes on something that is not a native input.

One hyphen, which is the limit of what React binds on a custom element.
`onhelix-change` reaches this; `onhelix-value-change`, which this was called,
reached nothing, because React stops at one hyphen and binds no event whose
name carries two.

The prefix is what keeps it clear of the native `change`. A consumer writes
`onhelix-change` for this and `onChange` for a real input's own, and the two
cannot be confused for each other. A control wrapping a native input relays
that input's `change` under its own name as well.
declarations.name: HelixChangeEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when something being previewed writes to the console.

Carries text rather than the logged values. The preview is a separate
document, so what arrives has crossed `postMessage` and been through
structured clone: a DOM node or a function does not survive that, and half a
value is worse than a string of it.
declarations.name: HelixConsoleEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when the cursor moves in a text editor.

Not cancelable, unlike everything else here. The others announce something
about to happen and a listener can refuse it; this one reports where the
caret already is, and there is nothing left to refuse.

It fires on every keystroke and every arrow press, which is why the status
bar reads it from the DOM rather than through a framework's state: routing a
caret position through React would re-render the workbench on every cursor
move.
declarations.name: HelixCaretEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when a component moves the view it is showing, rather than its value.

A calendar paging to another month is not choosing a date, and the two have
to be separable: a consumer driving the view needs to hear that it moved
without being told the answer changed. `helix-change` belongs to the value,
and giving it both jobs would make either one unusable on its own.
declarations.name: HelixNavigateEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when a component narrows what it is showing.

Filtering hides rather than removes, so nothing about the value changes and
`helix-change` would be a lie. What a consumer wants to know is that the list
in front of the reader is no longer the whole list.
declarations.name: HelixFilterEvent

declarations.description:
Owns only what is universal: normalizing `box-sizing` inside the shadow root,
so component CSS can rely on border-box on both sides of the boundary.

There is deliberately no `emit(name, detail)` helper. A dispatch through a
generic helper cannot be named by the manifest analyzer, which recorded the
parameter identifier and produced a phantom event on every element that
inherited it. Components dispatch concrete event classes from `events.ts`,
which the analyzer and TypeScript can both see.
declarations.name: HelixElement

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

declarations.description:
This has to be a class rather than a mixin or controller, and that is not a
style preference: the browser reads `formAssociated` off the constructor
during element upgrade, which cannot be delegated to a composed object.

`internals` comes from `HelixElement`, which attaches it for every component.
`attachInternals()` throws on a second call, so there is exactly one owner.

Deliberately small. It carries what every form participant needs and nothing
more; `value`, validity, and the reset and restore callbacks land when the
first input does, rather than being designed against components that do not
exist yet.

The consumer's callback, invoked after the change is applied.

Not reachable from React's JSX, which reserves every `on[A-Z]` prop for its
own event system; the generated wrapper listens for the event instead.

members.name: active
members.description:
Which item is current, by its `value`.

Reading gives the real one, in either mode. Writing hands ownership to the
consumer: from then on the set announces changes and applies none of them.

members.name: defaultActive
members.description: Initial item for uncontrolled use. Ignored once `active` is written.

members.name: requestActive
members.description: Requests a new current item, and reports whether the request stood.

members.name: resolveActive
members.description:
Which item is current, given what there is to choose from.

The first enabled one when `value` names nothing, which is a set before its
consumer has chosen and a set whose current item has just been removed.

declarations.description:
Grafts "which one of these is the current one" onto a container.

For a set where one member is current and the set is not a form control:
tabs, a tree, a nav bar, a carousel. Where it *is* a form control the value
is submitted and belongs to `MixinControllerValue`, which is why these are
two mixins and not one with a flag.

**Announcing before applying is the part worth sharing.** `Tabs` and `Tree`
both wrote the current value straight from the item's event, so a consumer
had no way to refuse a change, while `Radio.Group` announced first. Neither
was wrong on its own and the two together are: whether a selection can be
refused should not depend on which component a reader is looking at.

**The fallback is the other half.** Four components had written
`items.find(match) ?? items[0]`, and it is not the obvious line it looks
like: it is what makes a set with a `value` naming nothing still show
something, which is every set before its consumer has set one and every set
whose current item has just been removed. `resolveActive` also skips disabled
items, which the hand-written copies did not, so a set opening on a disabled
first item showed it as current.
declarations.name: MixinControllerActive

members.description:
Which item is current, by its `value`.

Called `active`, which is what this mixin is named for and what it was
not: it declared `value`, so the one mixin whose whole subject is which
item is active had no such property, and `active` meant something else
entirely elsewhere in the library. It still does, and only there now:
`option.active` is the option the keyboard is on, which is a different
question from which one is chosen.

An accessor pair, the same shape as the other three. Reading gives the
real item; writing hands ownership to the consumer, so `<helix-tabs
active="one">` is a set that stays on that tab and `default-active` is
how markup says where to start.

members.description:

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is

its consumer has chosen and a set whose current item has just been
removed. Disabled items are skipped in the fallback but not in the match:
a consumer who names a disabled item meant it, and quietly moving to
another would be the component overruling them.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

what it does not recognize; the generated wrapper listens for the events
instead.

What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

Reading gives the real value, in either mode. Writing hands ownership to
the consumer: from then on the control announces changes and applies none
of them, and waits to be told.

Not reachable from React's JSX, which reserves every `on[A-Z]` prop for its
own event system; the generated wrapper listens for `helix-change` instead.

declarations.description:
Grafts `value`, `defaultValue`, and the two callbacks that answer a form.

Every control with a value had written this, and by the third it was three
copies of the same four members and the same seeding rule: `Input`, then
`Toggle.Group`, then `Radio.Group`. The copies had not diverged, which is the
argument for the mixin rather than against it, because the next one would
have.

**Seeded in `willUpdate`, not `connectedCallback`.** SSR never calls the
latter, so a control with a `default-value` would serve empty and fill itself
at hydration, which is a flash for a reader and a mismatch for React. Seeding
once, before the first render, is what makes the server and the client agree.

**What it does not own is reporting.** `setFormValue` stays with the
component, because what an empty value means is the component's business: a
text field submits its emptiness, since `""` is an answer and the field was
on the form, while a group with nothing chosen submits nothing at all. One
mixin cannot hold both without a flag, and a flag would be this rule written
down twice.

`Checkbox` deliberately does not take this. Its `value` is what it submits
*when it is on* rather than what it holds, so it is configuration rather than
state, and the state it does have is `checked`, which is
`MixinControllerChecked`'s.
declarations.name: MixinControllerValue

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control

members.name: onValueChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the value is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. `onValueChange` and not `onChange`,
because React reserves the latter for its own synthetic system and wires
it to the native `change`, so a Helix event named `Change` would never
fire at all.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is

updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.description: Announces that it should go, and reports whether the request stood.

members.description: The event, built but not dispatched, for a caller that owns the timing.

declarations.description:
Grafts `dismissible`, its label, and the event that says so.

Three surfaces had written this: `Announcement`, `Tag` and `Toast.Item`, each
with the same two properties, the same event, and the same expression for the
label. They had not diverged, which is the argument for extracting rather than
against it, because the fourth would have.

**The label reads the default slot, not the whole element**, and that is a bug
fix rather than a move. Every copy said `this.textContent`, which is every
light-DOM descendant including the ones assigned elsewhere. On `Announcement`
and `Tag` that is the same thing, because they have one slot. On `Toast.Item`
it swept in the actions: a message reading "Could not reach the server" with a
`Retry` button announced itself as "Could not reach the server Retry", and the
consumer removing it from their list got that string to match on.

**`dismissEvent()` is separate from `dismiss()` for the one that needs it.**
`Announcement` and `Tag` dispatch and are done: they own no state, so a
refusal is the whole of the consumer's answer. `Toast.Item` holds an `open`
it may or may not own, so its event has to go through the controlled-change
path with an `apply` beside it. Giving it the event rather than the method
lets it keep the contract and skip the default.

reachable only as `dismisslabel`, which nobody would guess and no linter
would catch.

declarations.description:
Grafts a label, help text, and a validation message onto a control.

**Over `HelixElement` rather than `HelixFormElement`, because not every
control that wants a label is form-associated.** A checkbox group is the
case: each box in it submits itself already, so the group deliberately
reports no value of its own, and every form-related member of
`ElementInternals` throws `NotSupportedError` on an element that is not
form-associated. Measured, and the ARIA members are fine on the same
element, which is why the naming and describing work there and only the
validity has to ask first.

Every form control wants the same three things around it and wants them in a
different arrangement: a label above an input, beside a checkbox, and over a
group. So this owns the properties, the parts, and the wiring, and each
control places the nodes where its own geometry needs them. Same part names
either way, so one stylesheet in the styled tier dresses all of them.

**Not a wrapping `Field` component, and that is not a style preference.** A
wrapper cannot name what it wraps. Its label would live in its own shadow
root and the control in another, and measured in Chrome 148: an
`aria-labelledby` IDREF cannot see across, and
`control.ariaLabelledByElements = [labelInTheWrapper]` reads back as zero
elements, the reference dropped. The same assignment with a label in the
control's own tree is kept. That pattern works in React libraries because
they have no shadow boundary; bringing it here brings the ergonomics and none
of the conditions that made it work.

**A control whose label is its content renders its own.** A checkbox is named
by the words beside it, inside the `<label>` that forwards the press, so it
uses its default slot and nesting `renderLabel`'s `<label>` in there would be
invalid markup. `label` is that slot's fallback either way.

Worth knowing, because it costs a label and gives no warning: **a
whitespace-only text node is assigned to the default slot and defeats its
fallback.** Measured in Chrome 148, and a newline between the tags is enough,
so `<helix-checkbox label="Accept">` closed on the next line renders no label
at all. A named slot does not have this problem, because `slot="label"` is an
attribute and a text node has none. It is the platform's behavior rather
than ours, and the same is already true of every slot fallback here.

**The ids are fixed rather than generated.** IDREFs resolve within the tree
that holds them, so two controls on a page each carrying `helix-hint` in
their own shadow root do not collide. That also removes the usual hydration
hazard, since there is no generated value for a server and a client to
disagree about.

**A group has to say it differently.** A control's `<input>` and its hint
are both in the shadow root, so a plain `aria-describedby` resolves. A
group's host is in the light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot
reach and `element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference. Only
`internals.ariaDescribedByElements` keeps it, which is what `describeHost`
uses. Measured the same way, and the failure is silent either way: the
description simply never reaches the accessibility tree.
declarations.name: MixinField

members.name: touched

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this

reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

attributes.name: hint
attributes.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

attributes.name: feedback
attributes.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

attributes.name: required
attributes.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

declarations.name: anchorElement
declarations.description:
The element a floating surface should open against, given the slot it wraps.

**A wrapper with no box is not an anchor.** `display: contents` puts an
element's children into the layout and leaves the element itself without a
box, so its `getBoundingClientRect()` is `0 0 0 0`. Measured: a tooltip host
reports exactly that while the button inside it reports 32 by 32. Anchoring
to it opens the surface against the top left of the window, and focusing it
on close puts focus nowhere.

That is not an edge case, because wrapping is how a tooltip attaches to the
thing it describes. Without this, an icon button used as a trigger is the one
button on a toolbar that cannot have a tooltip.

So this descends past anything that draws nothing, and the first child with a
box is the anchor. The wrapper is transparent by construction, so the thing
with the box is the thing the reader is pointing at.

Bounded rather than a walk to the leaves: a chain of box-less wrappers is
already unusual, and descending without a limit through a tree this library
does not own is worse than stopping and anchoring to something imperfect.

declarations.name: closestInstance
declarations.description:
The nearest ancestor that is an instance of a class, crossing shadow roots.

**Identity rather than tag name, and the rule already existed.** `Accordion`'s
root states it two files from a violation of it: "Items are matched with
`instanceof`, never by tag name. Matching `helix-accordion-item` would tie
this tier to the styled one." Nine headless families resolve their
relationships that way; two did it by tag, and both named `helix-*` tags that
only `@helix-io/web` registers, which is a headless package depending on a
styled one by string.

The consequence is silent rather than loud. Subclassing a base element under
a different tag is exactly what the headless tier exists to allow, and it is
what `helix/web` itself does. Under a third tag the lookup returned `null`,
so an accordion's `mode` was ignored and every section behaved as `multiple`
with no error anywhere.

**`closest()` alone is not enough**, which is why this walks rather than
delegating. `closest()` stops at a shadow boundary: a component slotted into
another component's shadow root has a `parentNode` chain that ends at a
`ShadowRoot`, and `closest` will not step across it. Following `host` is what
makes a nested arrangement resolve, and nesting through a slot is the
ordinary case for anything composable.

declarations.name: createSheet
declarations.description:
Builds a stylesheet from CSS authored in a `.css` file.

Component styles live in real `.css` files rather than `css` tagged
templates, so they get CSS tooling: syntax highlighting, formatters, the
token linter, and a diff that reads as CSS. `bun run styles` compiles each
one into a sibling `.css.ts` that calls this.

The `unsafe` in `unsafeCSS` warns about interpolating untrusted input into a
stylesheet. That is not what happens here: the argument is a build-time
constant read from a file in this repo, never a runtime value. Wrapping it
keeps the warning where it belongs, on `unsafeCSS` itself, and gives one seam
to change if constructable stylesheets become the better primitive.

declarations.name: customElement
declarations.description:
Registers a custom element, once.

A drop-in replacement for Lit's `@customElement` that does not throw when the
tag is already registered.

The duplicate is not hypothetical. Next.js evaluates a module in both the
server and client graphs, so a component imported by a server component and a
client component runs its registration twice against one registry, and
`customElements.define` throws:

> Failed to execute 'define': the name "helix-card" has already been used

That failure takes down the whole prerender, and it appears only once an app
mixes server and client usage of the same component, which is exactly what a
real app does.

The analyzer detects `@customElement` **by decorator name**, not by where it
is imported from, so the manifest still records `tagName` and nothing
downstream changes.

declarations.name: focusableElements
declarations.description:
Everything inside `root` the reader can reach with Tab, in document order.

Separate from the focus trap because finding is the half most callers want:
roving tabindex, arrow-key navigation and "focus the first thing" all need
this list and none of them traps anything.

Visibility is tested with `getClientRects()` rather than `offsetParent`,
which is null for anything inside a `position: fixed` container. A drawer is
exactly that, so the `offsetParent` test excluded every control in the thing
being trapped.

declarations.name: deepActiveElement
declarations.description:
The truly focused element, following shadow roots down.

`document.activeElement` stops at the outermost host, so a button inside two
shadow roots reports as the component rather than as itself.

declarations.name: hostAria
declarations.description:
Writes a host's semantics onto its `ElementInternals`.

Onto internals rather than onto the host, which is the whole point: an
attribute written at upgrade is markup a React consumer's server output never
had, and hydration reports the difference. Internals carry the same meaning
to the accessibility tree and leave the element as the consumer wrote it.

**Empty means absent, and that is the trap this exists for.** Assigning `''`
to `ariaLabel` is not the same as not naming the element: it is a name of no
characters, which a screen reader announces as an unnamed control while every
check for "is it labelled" passes. Every caller had written
`this.label === '' ? null : this.label` and one of them would eventually not.

**Element references are feature-tested rather than assumed.** They are the
only way a host in the light DOM can point at a node in its own shadow root,
an IDREF cannot cross that boundary, and the plain `element.aria*Elements`
reflection drops the reference where `ElementInternals` keeps it. Older
engines have neither, and assigning to a property they do not implement is a
silent no-op rather than an error, so the guard is what makes the absence
visible to anything reading this.

Omitted keys are left alone, so a component that sets its role once in
`willUpdate` and its references later in `updated` does not have to repeat
itself or risk clearing what the other call wrote.

declarations.name: inheritDisabled
declarations.description:
Disables a group's members without forgetting what they said themselves.

A group and its members are two sources for one fact: a member is out of play
if either says so. Written the obvious way that is
`item.disabled = group || item.disabled`, and it latches. The first pass with
the group disabled writes `true` onto every member; the next pass reads its
own writing back as the member's own answer; and enabling the group leaves
every member disabled for good. Nothing about it is visible until something
re-enables a group, which is rare enough to ship and miserable to find.

So what a member said itself is recorded before it is first overridden, and
given back when the group lets go. Restoring is the half that matters: a
version that only recorded would read the overridden value as the member's
own the moment the group was enabled, which is the same latch by a longer
route.

Once given back, the record is dropped, so a consumer disabling a member
afterwards is its own answer again and is left alone.

declarations.name: forgetDisabled
declarations.description:
Forgets what a group recorded about an item.

For an item leaving a group, which would otherwise carry the group's last
word into wherever it goes next.

declarations.name: requestControlledChange

parameters.name:
{
  apply,
  controlled,
  event,
  host,
  label,
  notify,
  next,
  read,
}

declarations.description:
Announces a change, then applies it if nobody refused.

One audited path for every stateful change in the system. The order is the
whole point: the event goes first and carries the state being *proposed*, so
a listener calling `preventDefault()` stops it before anything moves. A
component that mutated itself and then announced it would leave a consumer
reacting to a decision already made.

Returns whether the change was applied, so a caller that needs to know
(a key handler deciding whether to also move focus) can ask.

A throwing `notify` is caught and logged rather than rethrown. A consumer's
broken callback must not corrupt the element's state or abort the rest of a
coordinated update, and there is nothing useful this can do about it besides
make it visible.

declarations.name: resolveActiveItem
declarations.description:
Which item a value names, or the first that could stand in for it.

`items.find(match) ?? items[0]` was written by hand in four components and it
is not the obvious line it looks like. It is what makes a set whose `value`
names nothing still show something, which is every set before its consumer
has chosen and every set whose current item has just been removed.

The fallback skips disabled items and the match does not. A consumer who
names a disabled item meant it, and quietly moving to another would be the
component overruling them; but falling back *onto* a disabled item is the
component choosing, and it should not choose something out of play. Every
hand-written copy took `items[0]` either way, so a set opening on a disabled
first item showed it as current.

A plain function rather than only a method on `MixinControllerActive`,
because the components that need it are split across two mixins: a set whose
value is submitted takes `MixinControllerValue` and cannot also take the
active one without two properties called `value`.

declarations.name: scrollItemIntoView
declarations.description:
Brings an item into view inside its own scroller, and moves nothing else.

**Not `Element.scrollIntoView`, and the difference is the whole reason this
exists.** That method walks every scrollable ancestor and scrolls all of
them, so bringing the current item into a tree also scrolls the page the tree
sits on, and on a phone it takes the address bar with it. A reader who
pressed Down in a sidebar did not ask the document to move.

It also does nothing when the item is already visible, where `scrollIntoView`
with `block: 'nearest'` still nudges. Nudging on every keypress is what makes
a long list feel like it is fighting the reader.

Both axes, because the components that need this do not agree on one: a
carousel scrolls sideways and a tree scrolls down, and a menu that has run
out of room does both.

`smooth` is a request rather than an instruction. Animating a scroll the
reader triggered by pressing a key means the list is still moving when the
next press arrives, so this follows `prefers-reduced-motion` and is off by
default for exactly that case.

declarations.name: SEVERITIES
declarations.default: { danger: { icon: xCircleFill, label: 'Error' }, info: { icon: infoFill, label: 'Information' }, success: { icon: checkCircleFill, label: 'Success' }, warning: { icon: warningFill, label: 'Warning' }, }
declarations.description:
The one severity vocabulary.

It was two, defined identically in `Callout` and in `Toast.Item`, and only one
of the copies carried the comment saying the two must not drift. A reader
meets these marks in a passage and in a message and has to read them as the
same four things, so there is one place they come from.

**Filled at every severity**, which is what it already was at one of them.
`danger` took `xCircleFill` and the other three took outlines, so a set meant
to be read as one vocabulary had one member drawn a different way. Filled
because a severity mark is a status indicator and not an action: it wants to
read at a glance and at a small size, where an outline at this weight loses
its interior.

**The label is not the severity name.** `danger` is announced as "Error",
because that is the word a reader understands and `danger` is the word the API
uses. Both matter and they are not the same string.

declarations.name: severityMark
declarations.description:
The mark for a severity, or `undefined` where the name is not one.

A lookup rather than direct indexing, because `severity` reaches a component
as an attribute and an attribute can say anything. Callers decide what an
unknown one means: `Callout` falls back to `info`, since a callout is always
*about* something, and `Toast.Item` draws nothing, since a message is just the
next thing that happened.
